problem: Socially-compliant navigation methods are evaluated with inconsistent experimental setups and mostly robot-centered metrics (RCM), which are hard to reproduce and unclear in how well they reflect human perception of social compatibility.
motivation: People fear or feel uneasy around robots whose behavior is unpredictable, so service robots in shared spaces need to be judged on human perception. Human questionnaires are costly and cannot be run in simulation, so it matters to know which cheap RCM actually track human-centered metrics (HCM).
key_idea: An end-to-end, reproducible real-robot benchmark that pairs a task-based human-robot experiment (carrying boxes) with the RoSAS questionnaire, then correlates RoSAS scores with robot-centered metrics to find which RCM proxy social compatibility.
insight: Only the robot extra time ratio (inversely) and the extra distance ratio track the human ratings. TDP, with pedestrian prediction, gets the best RoSAS scores (warmth 0.45, competence 0.65, discomfort 0.35) even though it has the lowest R^r_extra (0.74), because it waits rather than dodging. CADRL, which has the best R^r_extra and R_succ, is rated worst because it freezes. Safety-style metrics such as success ratio do not reflect human feelings at the low 0.3 m/s speed. The per-metric correlations are weak, and the paper itself notes the relationship is likely non-linear.
method: Experiment design: in a 2.5x4 m room a participant carries three cartons between two points while the robot shuttles between R1 and R2 four times, either along the human's path (passing/overtaking) or perpendicular to it (crossing). Max speed and acceleration are fixed at 0.3 m/s and 0.3 m/s².
Human-centered metrics: the 18-item RoSAS questionnaire (warmth, competence, discomfort; 1-9 scale). Internal consistency is validated with Cronbach's alpha of 0.94, 0.94 and 0.92.
Robot-centered metrics: robot extra time ratio, human extra time ratio (newly proposed), extra distance ratio, success ratio, hazard ratio (D_safe 0.2 m, D_social 0.4 m) and deceleration ratio.
Evaluated methods: Social Navigation Layers (SNL), Time Dependent Planning (TDP), CADRL (ROS implementation), move_base (MB), plus human-human (HH) interaction as a reference.

Platform and protocol: Clearpath Jackal with 4 RGB-D cameras, a 3D lidar and a 2D lidar under ROS; 20 participants with Latin-square counterbalancing of methods; one-way ANOVA and correlation analysis between RCM and HCM.

setting.backbone: Evaluated navigation stacks: SNL, TDP, move_base (classical cost-map planners) and CADRL (deep RL policy). The paper proposes no model of its own.
setting.training_data: none (benchmark paper; CADRL uses its released pretrained policy)
setting.observation: RGB-D cameras (4, panoramic), 3D lidar for people detection and tracking, 2D lidar for localization and obstacle avoidance

numbers_note: Not a standard navigation benchmark; metrics are RoSAS factors and robot-centered ratios (Table 2 and Table 3), so no benchmark entries were extracted.
results: With 20 participants, TDP scores best among robot methods on RoSAS (warmth 0.45, competence 0.65, discomfort 0.35), CADRL worst (0.30 / 0.40 / 0.60), and human-human interaction scores higher than all robots. Robot extra time ratio and extra distance ratio are recommended as proxies for social compatibility, while success, hazard and deceleration ratios are not.
limitations: Small sample (20 volunteers, mostly male university members), a small room, a single low robot speed (0.3 m/s), and one task type
Only four methods were tested, and the open-source CADRL freezes, which confounds the comparison
Correlations between RCM and HCM are weak and likely non-linear, so the RCM recommendation rests on limited evidence
